nodes.name: Acre-foot
nodes.currentDefinition: The volume of water covering one acre to a depth of one foot: 43 560 cubic feet (about 1233.5 m³).
nodes.currentSource: NIST Handbook 44, Appendix C.

definitions.value: The volume of water covering one acre to a depth of one foot: 43 560 cubic feet (about 1233.5 m³).
definitions.source: NIST Handbook 44, Appendix C.

nodes.etymology: Literally an acre of area times a foot of depth.
nodes.cursedness: The working unit of water rights in the western US. Roughly what one or two suburban households use in a year.

nodes.name: Acre
nodes.currentDefinition: One furlong by one chain: 4840 square yards (43 560 square feet), exactly 4046.856 422 4 m².
nodes.currentSource: Statute for Measuring Land (c. 1305); International Yard and Pound Agreement (1959); NIST Handbook 44, Appendix C; Weights and Measures Act 1985 (UK), Schedule 1.

definitions.value: One furlong by one chain: 4840 square yards (43 560 square feet), exactly 4046.856 422 4 m².
definitions.source: Statute for Measuring Land (c. 1305); International Yard and Pound Agreement (1959); NIST Handbook 44, Appendix C; Weights and Measures Act 1985 (UK), Schedule 1.

nodes.etymology: From Old English 'æcer', a field: the land a yoke of oxen could plough in a day.
nodes.cursedness: An acre is a furlong long and a chain wide, the shape of a ploughed strip. It has no simple relation to the square mile except that 640 acres make one. The US kept a slightly larger 'survey acre' (based on the survey foot) for land records until 2022.

nodes.name: Ampere
nodes.currentDefinition: Defined by fixing the numerical value of the elementary charge e to 1.602176634×10⁻¹⁹ coulombs, where the coulomb is ampere-seconds.
nodes.currentSource: 26th CGPM (2018), Resolution 1; BIPM SI Brochure, 9th ed. (2019), sec. 2.3.3.

definitions.value: That constant current which, if maintained in two straight parallel conductors of infinite length and negligible cross-section, placed 1 metre apart in vacuum, would produce a force of 2×10⁻⁷ newtons per metre of length between them.
definitions.source: CIPM (1946), Resolution 2; confirmed by 9th CGPM (1948).

definitions.value: Defined by fixing the numerical value of the elementary charge e to 1.602176634×10⁻¹⁹ coulombs, where the coulomb is ampere-seconds.
definitions.source: 26th CGPM (2018), Resolution 1; BIPM SI Brochure, 9th ed. (2019), sec. 2.3.3.

nodes.etymology: Named after André-Marie Ampère, French physicist and a founder of electromagnetism.
nodes.cursedness: The 2019 definition fixes the elementary charge e, which is a charge, not a current, in coulombs (ampere-seconds). Solving for the ampere gives 1 A = e / (1.602176634×10⁻¹⁹ s), so this 'base' unit actually rests on the second. The elementary charge would most naturally define the coulomb, with no second needed (1 C = e / 1.602176634×10⁻¹⁹), and the ampere would then be the derived unit, C/s. The SI kept the ampere as the base unit for historical reasons: its 1946–2019 definition used the force between two current-carrying wires, which made current the quantity labs could measure directly. When the 2019 redefinition switched to fixing e, the ampere stayed the base unit and the coulomb stayed derived. That leaves the definition reading in a circle: it states e in coulombs, 'which is equal to A s', so the ampere is defined through a unit built from the ampere. It isn't a true loop, because the fixed value of e pins the ampere down. But the IEC's terminology committee has pointed out that all seven 2019 definitions read circularly as worded, and that they can't be copied verbatim into a terminology standard (Mari et al., 2019).

nodes.name: Apothecaries' dram
nodes.currentDefinition: Three scruples (60 grains, about 3.888 g): 1/8 of an apothecaries' ounce.
nodes.currentSource: British Pharmacopoeia (abandoned on metrication, 1971); NIST Handbook 44, Appendix C.

definitions.value: Three scruples (60 grains, about 3.888 g): 1/8 of an apothecaries' ounce.
definitions.source: British Pharmacopoeia (abandoned on metrication, 1971); NIST Handbook 44, Appendix C.

nodes.etymology: From Greek 'drachmē'.
nodes.cursedness: More than twice the avoirdupois dram, under the same name. Prescriptions written with the ʒ symbol were a classic source of dosing errors.

nodes.name: Arcminute
nodes.currentDefinition: A unit of plane angle equal to 1/60 degree (π/10 800 radian). Accepted for use with the SI, where it is simply called the minute.
nodes.currentSource: CIPM (1969); BIPM SI Brochure, 9th ed. (2019), Table 8.

definitions.value: A unit of plane angle equal to 1/60 degree (π/10 800 radian). Accepted for use with the SI, where it is simply called the minute.
definitions.source: CIPM (1969); BIPM SI Brochure, 9th ed. (2019), Table 8.

nodes.etymology: The same 'first small part' (pars minuta prima) as the minute of time; 'arc' distinguishes it.
nodes.cursedness: The SI Brochure calls it just the 'minute', the same name as the unit of time, which is why everyone else says arcminute. The nautical mile was originally one arcminute of latitude.

nodes.name: Arcsecond
nodes.currentDefinition: A unit of plane angle equal to 1/60 arcminute (π/648 000 radian). Accepted for use with the SI, where it is simply called the second.
nodes.currentSource: CIPM (1969); BIPM SI Brochure, 9th ed. (2019), Table 8.

definitions.value: A unit of plane angle equal to 1/60 arcminute (π/648 000 radian). Accepted for use with the SI, where it is simply called the second.
definitions.source: CIPM (1969); BIPM SI Brochure, 9th ed. (2019), Table 8.

nodes.etymology: From 'pars minuta secunda', the 'second small part' of a degree — the same root as the second of time.
nodes.cursedness: The SI Brochure names it the 'second', the same as the SI base unit of time. Astronomers put prefixes on it (mas, µas) even though the symbol ″ is not a letter. The parsec is defined from it: the distance at which 1 au subtends one arcsecond.

nodes.name: Astronomical unit
nodes.currentDefinition: Exactly 149 597 870 700 metres. Accepted for use with the SI.
nodes.currentSource: IAU (2012), Resolution B2; BIPM SI Brochure, 9th ed. (2019), Table 8.

definitions.value: The radius of an unperturbed circular orbit around the Sun of a body of negligible mass moving at a mean angular speed of 0.017 202 098 95 radian per day (the Gaussian gravitational constant), measured at about 149 597 870 700 m.
definitions.source: IAU (1976), Resolution 10.

definitions.value: Exactly 149 597 870 700 metres. Accepted for use with the SI.
definitions.source: IAU (2012), Resolution B2; BIPM SI Brochure, 9th ed. (2019), Table 8.

nodes.etymology: Originally the mean distance between the Earth and the Sun, the natural yardstick of the solar system.
nodes.cursedness: For centuries it was the Earth–Sun distance, then a dynamical length tied to the Gaussian gravitational constant, which made its value in metres depend on which relativistic time scale you used. In 2012 the IAU gave up and set it to a fixed number of metres. Its symbol was variously AU, ua and a.u.; the IAU and BIPM settled on 'au' only in 2012–2014.

nodes.name: Barleycorn
nodes.currentDefinition: One third of an inch. Originally the length of a grain of barley; now exactly 1/3 in.
nodes.currentSource: Composition of Yards and Perches (c. 1300); defined from the inch since 1959.

definitions.value: One third of an inch. Originally the length of a grain of barley; now exactly 1/3 in.
definitions.source: Composition of Yards and Perches (c. 1300); defined from the inch since 1959.

nodes.etymology: From the grain of barley, the oldest English length standard.
nodes.cursedness: The inch was originally defined as three barleycorns, so the barleycorn was the base of the whole English length system. It survives only in UK and US shoe sizes, where each full size is one barleycorn longer than the last.

nodes.name: Becquerel
nodes.currentDefinition: The activity of a radionuclide decaying at a rate of one spontaneous nuclear transition per second.
nodes.currentSource: 15th CGPM (1975), Resolution 8; BIPM SI Brochure, 9th ed. (2019), Table 4.

definitions.value: The activity of a radionuclide decaying at a rate of one spontaneous nuclear transition per second.
definitions.source: 15th CGPM (1975), Resolution 8; BIPM SI Brochure, 9th ed. (2019), Table 4.

nodes.etymology: Named after Henri Becquerel, who discovered radioactivity in uranium salts in 1896.
nodes.cursedness: Dimensionally identical to the hertz, but the SI forbids using one for the other: the becquerel counts random decay events, while the hertz counts cycles of a periodic phenomenon. The SI Brochure restricts the hertz to periodic phenomena and the becquerel to radioactive decay, and the CGPM gave activity its own name in 1975 so that mistakes in radiation measurements couldn't endanger human health. See the hertz-becquerel relationship. It replaced the curie (3.7 × 10¹⁰ Bq, roughly the activity of one gram of radium-226), which is still widely used in the US.

nodes.name: Board foot
nodes.currentDefinition: A board one foot long, one foot wide and one inch thick: 144 cubic inches (about 2.36 L). Used for lumber.
nodes.currentSource: NIST Handbook 44, Appendix C.

definitions.value: A board one foot long, one foot wide and one inch thick: 144 cubic inches (about 2.36 L). Used for lumber.
definitions.source: NIST Handbook 44, Appendix C.

nodes.etymology: From the sawn board.
nodes.cursedness: Lumber is measured by its nominal size before drying and planing, so a '2×4' is really 1½ × 3½ inches, but board feet are still worked out from the nominal 2 × 4.

nodes.name: British thermal unit
nodes.currentDefinition: The International Table Btu: exactly 1055.055 852 62 joules.
nodes.currentSource: Fifth International Conference on the Properties of Steam (London, 1956).

definitions.value: The heat needed to raise the temperature of one pound of water by one degree Fahrenheit. Its value depended on the starting temperature, giving 39 °F, 59 °F, 60 °F and 'mean' Btus.
definitions.source: Historical engineering usage.

definitions.value: The International Table Btu: exactly 1055.055 852 62 joules.
definitions.source: Fifth International Conference on the Properties of Steam (London, 1956).

nodes.etymology: Named for Britain, though it is now used mainly in the US for heating and air conditioning.
nodes.cursedness: There are at least six Btus that differ by up to 0.1 %. Air conditioners are rated in 'Btu', which actually means Btu per hour, a unit of power, and a 'ton' of cooling is 12 000 Btu/h, the cooling from melting a short ton of ice in a day.

nodes.name: Candela
nodes.currentDefinition: Defined by fixing the numerical value of the luminous efficacy of monochromatic radiation of frequency 540×10¹² Hz, K_cd, to 683 lumens per watt, where the lumen is cd·sr.
nodes.currentSource: 26th CGPM (2018), Resolution 1; BIPM SI Brochure, 9th ed. (2019), sec. 2.3.1.

definitions.value: Luminous intensity of a specified 'Planckian radiator' (blackbody) at the freezing temperature of platinum, per unit area, in a given direction (the 'new candle').
definitions.source: CIPM (1946), Resolution 2.

definitions.value: The luminous intensity, in a given direction, of a source that emits monochromatic radiation of frequency 540×10¹² Hz and has a radiant intensity in that direction of 1/683 watt per steradian.
definitions.source: 16th CGPM (1979), Resolution 3.

definitions.value: Defined by fixing the numerical value of the luminous efficacy of monochromatic radiation of frequency 540×10¹² Hz, K_cd, to 683 lumens per watt, where the lumen is cd·sr.
definitions.source: 26th CGPM (2018), Resolution 1; BIPM SI Brochure, 9th ed. (2019), sec. 2.3.1.

nodes.etymology: From Latin 'candela', meaning candle.
nodes.cursedness: The only SI base unit defined partly by human biology. Its constant, the luminous efficacy K_cd = 683 lm/W at 540 THz, comes from the peak sensitivity of the average human eye, not from physics. The definition also reads in a circle: it fixes K_cd in lumens per watt, but the lumen is cd·sr, so the candela is defined through a unit built from itself. The fixed value of K_cd pins it down anyway; the IEC's terminology committee has noted that all seven 2019 definitions read circularly as worded (Mari et al., 2019). Unpacked, the definition rests on the hertz, the steradian and the watt, so this 'base' unit actually depends on the kilogram, metre and second (the steradian is dimensionless). It is in effect a derived unit: radiant power per solid angle, weighted by a standardised eye.

nodes.name: Degree Celsius
nodes.currentDefinition: A unit of thermodynamic temperature equal in magnitude to the kelvin, with its zero point set at 273.15 K (the ice point of water) instead of absolute zero.
nodes.currentSource: 9th CGPM (1948); BIPM SI Brochure, 9th ed. (2019), sec. 2.3.4.

definitions.value: A unit of thermodynamic temperature equal in magnitude to the kelvin, with its zero point set at 273.15 K (the ice point of water) instead of absolute zero.
definitions.source: 9th CGPM (1948); BIPM SI Brochure, 9th ed. (2019), sec. 2.3.4.

nodes.etymology: Named after Anders Celsius, who proposed a related centigrade scale in 1742 (originally with the scale inverted — 0 at boiling, 100 at freezing).
nodes.cursedness: Same-sized degree as the kelvin, different zero — see the kelvin-celsius relationship for why they were historically conflated. Celsius's own original 1742 scale ran backwards from today's.

nodes.name: Chain
nodes.currentDefinition: Four rods (22 yards, 66 feet), exactly 20.1168 m: the length of Gunter's surveying chain of 100 links.
nodes.currentSource: International Yard and Pound Agreement (1959); NIST Handbook 44, Appendix C; Weights and Measures Act 1985 (UK), Schedule 1.

definitions.value: Four rods (22 yards, 66 feet), exactly 20.1168 m: the length of Gunter's surveying chain of 100 links.
definitions.source: International Yard and Pound Agreement (1959); NIST Handbook 44, Appendix C; Weights and Measures Act 1985 (UK), Schedule 1.

nodes.etymology: From the physical chain, introduced by the English mathematician Edmund Gunter in 1620.
nodes.cursedness: Gunter's chain made English land decimal: an acre is 10 square chains, and 100 links make a chain, so surveyors could do decimal arithmetic in a non-decimal system. A cricket pitch is still exactly one chain long.

nodes.name: Circular mil
nodes.currentDefinition: The area of a circle one mil (0.001 inch) in diameter: π/4 square mils, about 506.7 µm².
nodes.currentSource: NIST Handbook 44, Appendix C.

definitions.value: The area of a circle one mil (0.001 inch) in diameter: π/4 square mils, about 506.7 µm².
definitions.source: NIST Handbook 44, Appendix C.

nodes.etymology: Circular, because it measures circles: a wire d mils across has an area of exactly d² circular mils.
nodes.cursedness: It exists so electricians never have to multiply by π: square the diameter and you're done. US wire sizes above 4/0 AWG are given in kcmil (thousands of circular mils), also written MCM.

nodes.name: Cord
nodes.currentDefinition: 128 cubic feet of stacked firewood: a pile 8 ft long, 4 ft high and 4 ft deep, gaps included.
nodes.currentSource: NIST Handbook 44, Appendix C.

definitions.value: 128 cubic feet of stacked firewood: a pile 8 ft long, 4 ft high and 4 ft deep, gaps included.
definitions.source: NIST Handbook 44, Appendix C.

nodes.etymology: From the cord or string once used to measure the stack.
nodes.cursedness: Firewood sellers often sell a 'face cord' or 'rick', a single row that can be any depth, so it is a third or less of a real cord.

nodes.name: Coulomb
nodes.currentDefinition: The quantity of electricity carried in one second by a current of one ampere.
nodes.currentSource: CIPM (1946), Resolution 2; BIPM SI Brochure, 9th ed. (2019).

definitions.value: The quantity of electricity carried in one second by a current of one ampere.
definitions.source: CIPM (1946), Resolution 2; BIPM SI Brochure, 9th ed. (2019).

nodes.etymology: Named after Charles-Augustin de Coulomb, for his law of electrostatic force.

nodes.name: Dalton
nodes.currentDefinition: 1/12 of the mass of a free carbon-12 atom, at rest and in its ground state. Its value in kilograms is measured, not fixed: 1.660 539 068 92(52) × 10⁻²⁷ kg (CODATA 2022). Accepted for use with the SI.
nodes.currentSource: IUPAP and IUPAC (1960–1961); BIPM SI Brochure, 9th ed. (2019), Table 8; CODATA 2022.

definitions.value: 1/12 of the mass of a free carbon-12 atom, at rest and in its ground state. Its value in kilograms is measured, not fixed: 1.660 539 068 92(52) × 10⁻²⁷ kg (CODATA 2022). Accepted for use with the SI.
definitions.source: IUPAP and IUPAC (1960–1961); BIPM SI Brochure, 9th ed. (2019), Table 8; CODATA 2022.

nodes.etymology: Named after John Dalton, who proposed the atomic theory of matter. The symbol u comes from its older name, the 'unified atomic mass unit'.
nodes.cursedness: Before 2019, the mole was defined from carbon-12 too, so a mole of daltons was exactly one gram. The 2019 redefinition fixed the Avogadro constant instead, and that link is now only approximate, though still good to better than a part in a billion. Before 1961, physicists based their atomic mass unit on oxygen-16 and chemists on natural oxygen, so there were two units differing by about 0.03 %; the carbon-12 unit was the compromise.

nodes.name: Day
nodes.currentDefinition: A unit of time equal to 24 hours (86 400 seconds), accepted for use with the SI.
nodes.currentSource: CIPM (1969); BIPM SI Brochure, 9th ed. (2019), Table 8.

definitions.value: A unit of time equal to 24 hours (86 400 seconds), accepted for use with the SI.
definitions.source: CIPM (1969); BIPM SI Brochure, 9th ed. (2019), Table 8.

nodes.etymology: From Old English 'dæg'.
nodes.cursedness: The second was originally 1/86 400 of a mean solar day; now the day is defined as 86 400 seconds, and the Earth's actual rotation no longer matches. Tidal braking makes the solar day about 2 ms longer per century, which is why leap seconds were needed. The symbol d is also the deci prefix.

nodes.name: Degree
nodes.currentDefinition: A unit of plane angle equal to π/180 radian, so that a full turn is 360°. Accepted for use with the SI.
nodes.currentSource: CIPM (1969); BIPM SI Brochure, 9th ed. (2019), Table 8.

definitions.value: A unit of plane angle equal to π/180 radian, so that a full turn is 360°. Accepted for use with the SI.
definitions.source: CIPM (1969); BIPM SI Brochure, 9th ed. (2019), Table 8.

nodes.etymology: From Latin 'gradus', a step. The 360-part circle comes from Babylonian astronomy, probably via the roughly 360-day year and base-60 counting.
nodes.cursedness: With the arcminute and arcsecond, it is one of the only units accepted for use with the SI whose factor to its SI unit is irrational: 1° = π/180 rad, so no exact decimal exists. The symbol ° is also the one in °C, which is a different thing entirely.

nodes.name: Dram (avoirdupois)
nodes.currentDefinition: 1/16 of an avoirdupois ounce: about 1.771 845 g.
nodes.currentSource: International Yard and Pound Agreement (1959); NIST Handbook 44, Appendix C; Weights and Measures Act 1985 (UK), Schedule 1.

definitions.value: 1/16 of an avoirdupois ounce: about 1.771 845 g.
definitions.source: International Yard and Pound Agreement (1959); NIST Handbook 44, Appendix C; Weights and Measures Act 1985 (UK), Schedule 1.

nodes.etymology: From Greek 'drachmē', a coin and weight.
nodes.cursedness: The avoirdupois dram (1/16 oz) and the apothecaries' dram (1/8 apothecaries' ounce) differ by more than a factor of two, and there's a fluid dram too. 'A wee dram' of whisky is none of them.

nodes.name: Electronvolt
nodes.currentDefinition: The kinetic energy gained by an electron passing through a potential difference of one volt in vacuum: exactly 1.602 176 634 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, since the 2019 redefinition fixed the elementary charge. Accepted for use with the SI.
nodes.currentSource: BIPM SI Brochure, 9th ed. (2019), Table 8.

definitions.value: The kinetic energy gained by an electron passing through a potential difference of one volt in vacuum; its value in joules was measured.
definitions.source: BIPM SI Brochure, 8th ed. (2006), Table 7.

definitions.value: The kinetic energy gained by an electron passing through a potential difference of one volt in vacuum: exactly 1.602 176 634 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, since the 2019 redefinition fixed the elementary charge. Accepted for use with the SI.
definitions.source: BIPM SI Brochure, 9th ed. (2019), Table 8.

nodes.etymology: 'Electron' plus 'volt': the energy one electron's charge gains across one volt.
nodes.cursedness: Particle physicists quote masses in eV/c² and then drop the c², so the 'mass of the proton is 938 MeV'. In natural units, where c = 1, energy, mass, momentum and inverse length all end up in eV. Before 2019 its value in joules was measured; now it is exact, because the elementary charge is fixed.

nodes.name: Degree Fahrenheit
nodes.currentDefinition: Defined from the Celsius scale: t/°F = 1.8 · t/°C + 32, so water freezes at 32 °F and boils at 212 °F at standard pressure. A degree Fahrenheit is 5/9 of a kelvin, and 0 °F is 459.67 °R.
nodes.currentSource: NIST Handbook 44, Appendix C.

definitions.value: A scale with 0 °F at the temperature of a brine of ice, water and ammonium chloride and 96 °F at human body temperature; water froze at 32 °F.
definitions.source: D. G. Fahrenheit, Philosophical Transactions 33 (1724).

definitions.value: Defined from the Celsius scale: t/°F = 1.8 · t/°C + 32, so water freezes at 32 °F and boils at 212 °F at standard pressure. A degree Fahrenheit is 5/9 of a kelvin, and 0 °F is 459.67 °R.
definitions.source: NIST Handbook 44, Appendix C.

nodes.etymology: Named after Daniel Gabriel Fahrenheit, the German-Polish instrument maker who invented the mercury thermometer.
nodes.cursedness: Fahrenheit's fixed points didn't survive: after recalibration, body temperature came out at about 98.6 °F, not 96. It is now defined from the Celsius scale, which is defined from the kelvin, so the US measures temperature in a scale that depends on two others. Like the degree Celsius, it is a degree size and an offset, so 20 °F is not 'twice as hot' as 10 °F.

nodes.name: Farad
nodes.currentDefinition: The capacitance of a capacitor between the plates of which there appears a difference of potential of one volt when it is charged by a quantity of electricity of one coulomb.
nodes.currentSource: CIPM (1946), Resolution 2; BIPM SI Brochure, 9th ed. (2019).

definitions.value: The capacitance of a capacitor between the plates of which there appears a difference of potential of one volt when it is charged by a quantity of electricity of one coulomb.
definitions.source: CIPM (1946), Resolution 2; BIPM SI Brochure, 9th ed. (2019).

nodes.etymology: Named after Michael Faraday, for his contributions to electromagnetism and electrochemistry.

nodes.name: Fathom
nodes.currentDefinition: Two yards (six feet), exactly 1.8288 m. Used for the depth of water.
nodes.currentSource: International Yard and Pound Agreement (1959); NIST Handbook 44, Appendix C; Weights and Measures Act 1985 (UK), Schedule 1.

definitions.value: Two yards (six feet), exactly 1.8288 m. Used for the depth of water.
definitions.source: International Yard and Pound Agreement (1959); NIST Handbook 44, Appendix C; Weights and Measures Act 1985 (UK), Schedule 1.

nodes.etymology: From Old English 'fæthm', the outstretched arms — the span of a sailor's arms when hauling a sounding line.
nodes.cursedness: Nautical charts used fathoms for depth until metrication; the 'Mark Twain' pen name is a leadsman's call for two fathoms.

nodes.name: Foot-candle
nodes.currentDefinition: One lumen per square foot: about 10.764 lux.
nodes.currentSource: NIST Handbook 44, Appendix C.

definitions.value: One lumen per square foot: about 10.764 lux.
definitions.source: NIST Handbook 44, Appendix C.

nodes.etymology: The illuminance one foot from a standard candle, before the candle was replaced by the candela.
nodes.cursedness: Still the unit of US lighting codes and photography light meters, so a building can be designed in foot-candles and inspected in lux.

nodes.name: Foot
nodes.currentDefinition: Exactly 0.3048 metres (12 inches, 1/3 of the international yard).
nodes.currentSource: International Yard and Pound Agreement (1959); NIST Handbook 44, Appendix C; Weights and Measures Act 1985 (UK), Schedule 1.

definitions.value: 1/3 of the national standard yard. Its length depended on whose standard: the British, American (1893: 1200/3937 m) and others differed by a few parts per million.
definitions.source: Weights and Measures Act 1878 (UK); Mendenhall Order (US, 1893).

definitions.value: Exactly 0.3048 metres (12 inches, 1/3 of the international yard).
definitions.source: International Yard and Pound Agreement (1959); NIST Handbook 44, Appendix C; Weights and Measures Act 1985 (UK), Schedule 1.

nodes.etymology: From the human foot; Old English 'fōt'.
nodes.cursedness: Feet have ranged from about 25 cm to 34 cm across history and Europe; nearly every town once had its own. The Roman foot was about 29.6 cm. Even after 1959, the US kept a second foot for land surveying — see the US survey foot — and only retired it at the end of 2022.

nodes.name: Fortnight
nodes.currentDefinition: Fourteen days.
nodes.currentSource: Traditional English usage.

definitions.value: Fourteen days.
definitions.source: Traditional English usage.

nodes.etymology: From Old English 'fēowertīene niht', fourteen nights.
nodes.cursedness: Common in British English and almost unknown in American English. It anchors the joke FFF system (furlong, firkin, fortnight), in which the speed of light is about 1.8 × 10¹² furlongs per fortnight.

nodes.name: Furlong
nodes.currentDefinition: Ten chains (40 rods, 220 yards), exactly 201.168 m.
nodes.currentSource: Weights and Measures Act 1593 (35 Eliz. 1 c. 6); International Yard and Pound Agreement (1959); NIST Handbook 44, Appendix C; Weights and Measures Act 1985 (UK), Schedule 1.

definitions.value: Ten chains (40 rods, 220 yards), exactly 201.168 m.
definitions.source: Weights and Measures Act 1593 (35 Eliz. 1 c. 6); International Yard and Pound Agreement (1959); NIST Handbook 44, Appendix C; Weights and Measures Act 1985 (UK), Schedule 1.

nodes.etymology: From Old English 'furh lang', the length of a furrow in a common field.
nodes.cursedness: It began as the length a team of oxen could plough without resting, so it predates the mile and the mile was eventually stretched to fit it. Horse racing still uses it. The 'furlong per fortnight', about 0.17 mm/s, is the classic joke unit of speed.

nodes.name: Grain
nodes.currentDefinition: 1/7000 of a pound: exactly 64.798 91 milligrams.
nodes.currentSource: International Yard and Pound Agreement (1959); NIST Handbook 44, Appendix C; Weights and Measures Act 1985 (UK), Schedule 1.

definitions.value: 1/7000 of a pound: exactly 64.798 91 milligrams.
definitions.source: International Yard and Pound Agreement (1959); NIST Handbook 44, Appendix C; Weights and Measures Act 1985 (UK), Schedule 1.

nodes.etymology: From a grain of barley (or wheat) as a unit of weight.
nodes.cursedness: The one unit shared by the avoirdupois, troy and apothecaries' systems, which is how they connect: 7000 grains to the avoirdupois pound, 5760 to the troy pound. Still used for bullets, arrowheads and gunpowder.

nodes.name: Gray
nodes.currentDefinition: The absorbed dose of ionizing radiation corresponding to one joule of energy imparted per kilogram of matter.
nodes.currentSource: 15th CGPM (1975), Resolution 9; BIPM SI Brochure, 9th ed. (2019), Table 4.

definitions.value: The absorbed dose of ionizing radiation corresponding to one joule of energy imparted per kilogram of matter.
definitions.source: 15th CGPM (1975), Resolution 9; BIPM SI Brochure, 9th ed. (2019), Table 4.

nodes.etymology: Named after Louis Harold Gray, a British physicist who pioneered radiobiology and the measurement of absorbed dose.
nodes.cursedness: Shares its unit, J/kg, with the sievert and with specific energy in general, but the three are never interchangeable. See the gray-sievert relationship. It replaced the rad (0.01 Gy), which collides with the symbol of the radian.

nodes.name: Hand
nodes.currentDefinition: Four inches, used for the height of horses at the withers.
nodes.currentSource: Horses Act 1540 (32 Hen. 8); defined from the inch since 1959.

definitions.value: Four inches, used for the height of horses at the withers.

nodes.cursedness: Before 1959 the British, American and Canadian inches were all slightly different, by a few parts per million. The inch is now defined by the metre, so every customary length is a metric length in disguise.

nodes.name: Kelvin
nodes.currentDefinition: Defined by fixing the numerical value of the Boltzmann constant k to 1.380649×10⁻²³ J/K, where the joule is kg·m²·s⁻².

definitions.source: 26th CGPM (2018), Resolution 1; BIPM SI Brochure, 9th ed. (2019), sec. 2.3.4.

nodes.etymology: Named after William Thomson, 1st Baron Kelvin, who proposed an absolute temperature scale in 1848.
nodes.cursedness: The 2019 definition fixes the Boltzmann constant k in joules per kelvin, so temperature now rests on energy: 1 K is the temperature change that changes kT by 1.380649×10⁻²³ J. Because the joule is kg·m²·s⁻², this 'base' unit actually depends on the kilogram, metre and second. Temperature is in effect an energy per degree of freedom that the SI measures in a separate unit for historical reasons.

nodes.name: Kilogram
nodes.currentDefinition: Defined by fixing the numerical value of the Planck constant h to 6.62607015×10⁻³⁴ J·s, which is kg·m²·s⁻¹.
nodes.currentSource: 26th CGPM (2018), Resolution 1; BIPM SI Brochure, 9th ed. (2019), sec. 2.3.2.

definitions.value: Mass of the Kilogramme des Archives, a platinum artifact intended to equal the mass of one litre of water at its temperature of maximum density.

definitions.value: Mass of the International Prototype of the Kilogram (IPK), a platinum-iridium cylinder held at the BIPM.
definitions.source: 1st CGPM (1889), Resolution.

definitions.value: Defined by fixing the numerical value of the Planck constant h to 6.62607015×10⁻³⁴ J·s, which is kg·m²·s⁻¹.
definitions.source: 26th CGPM (2018), Resolution 1; BIPM SI Brochure, 9th ed. (2019), sec. 2.3.2.

nodes.etymology: From French 'kilogramme', from Greek 'khilioi' (thousand) + 'gramma' (small weight).
nodes.cursedness: The only SI base unit whose name contains a prefix ('kilo-'), a historical artifact of the gram being defined first and later found too small to be practical as the base unit. Since 2019, the definition fixes the Planck constant h in joule-seconds (kg·m²·s⁻¹), so the kilogram actually depends on the metre and second: 1 kg = h / (6.62607015×10⁻³⁴ m²·s⁻¹). Before 2019, the dependency ran the other way. The joule, newton and every other mechanical unit were tied to a metal cylinder in a vault in Sèvres, which slowly drifted in mass compared with its official copies. The 2019 wording also reads in a circle: it states h in joule-seconds, and the joule is N·m with N = kg·m/s², so the kilogram is defined through a unit built from the kilogram. Fixing h's value pins it down anyway, but the IEC's terminology committee singled the kilogram out as the hardest definition to rephrase in non-circular words (Mari et al., 2019).

High-precision volumes measured in that era have to be corrected. It has two official symbols, because a lowercase l is hard to tell from the digit 1; the CGPM added the capital L in 1979 as a deliberate exception to the rule that only units named after people get a capital.

nodes.name: Mile
nodes.currentDefinition: Exactly 1609.344 metres (5280 international feet).

definitions.value: Exactly 1609.344 metres (5280 international feet).

nodes.etymology: From Latin 'mille passus', a thousand paces (double steps) of a Roman legion.
nodes.cursedness: The Roman mile was 5000 Roman feet. The English mile became 5280 feet in 1593 only because Parliament wanted it to be a whole number of furlongs. 'Statute mile' distinguishes it from the nautical mile (1852 m), and until 2022 there was also a US survey mile, 3.2 mm longer.

nodes.name: Minute
nodes.currentDefinition: A unit of time equal to 60 seconds, accepted for use with the SI.
nodes.currentSource: CIPM (1969); BIPM SI Brochure, 9th ed. (2019), Table 8.

definitions.value: A unit of time equal to 60 seconds, accepted for use with the SI.

nodes.etymology: From Medieval Latin 'pars minuta prima', the 'first small part' of an hour in Babylonian-derived sexagesimal division.
nodes.cursedness: Not every minute has 60 seconds. When a leap second is inserted into UTC, that minute has 61 — and the 2022 decision to stop inserting leap seconds by 2035 means this is being phased out rather than fixed. The base-60 split itself comes from Babylonian astronomy.

nodes.name: Mole
nodes.currentDefinition: Defined by fixing the numerical value of the Avogadro constant N_A to 6.02214076×10²³ per mole.
nodes.currentSource: 26th CGPM (2018), Resolution 1; BIPM SI Brochure, 9th ed. (2019), sec. 2.3.5.

definitions.value: The amount of substance of a system which contains as many elementary entities as there are atoms in 0.012 kilogram of carbon-12.
definitions.source: 14th CGPM (1971), Resolution 3.

definitions.value: Defined by fixing the numerical value of the Avogadro constant N_A to 6.02214076×10²³ per mole.
definitions.source: 26th CGPM (2018), Resolution 1; BIPM SI Brochure, 9th ed. (2019), sec. 2.3.5.

nodes.etymology: From German 'Molekül', coined by Wilhelm Ostwald around 1900 as a short form of 'gram-molecule'.
nodes.cursedness: Whether the mole should be a unit at all is a matter of convention. Its defining constant, the Avogadro constant N_A = 6.02214076×10²³ mol⁻¹, is a quantity with a unit: entities per mole. Fixing it gives 1 mol = 6.02214076×10²³ / N_A, so the only unit involved is the mole itself, and like the second it depends on no other unit. Drop the unit and N_A becomes the Avogadro number, a plain count, and the mole becomes a counting word like 'dozen'. On that view, amount of substance is not a dimension at all. The SI keeps it as a separate base dimension so that chemistry stays dimensionally consistent, for example molar mass in kg/mol rather than just kg. This is the same kind of choice the SI makes in treating the radian as dimensionless. The mole also depended on the kilogram until 2019 (0.012 kg of carbon-12), so a change in the kilogram changed the mole. The 2019 redefinition removed that link.

The 42-gallon oil barrel came from the English wine tierce. Its symbol 'bbl' is often said to stand for 'blue barrel', but that story is unproven.

Confusing them is how the Mars Climate Orbiter was lost in 1999: one team's software reported impulse in pound-force seconds and another read it as newton-seconds. There are also troy and apothecaries' pounds of 12 ounces, used for precious metals and drugs.

nodes.name: Radian

nodes.etymology: From Latin 'radius'.
nodes.cursedness: The radian is a metre-per-metre ratio, so SI treats it as dimensionless and usually drops it from equations entirely — but this is a choice, not a necessity. There's a competing, equally valid convention where the number 1 means one full revolution (used for rpm etc.), off from the radian convention by a factor of 2π. Angular momentum and torque only end up sharing units with energy because SI's convention quietly discards the radian.

nodes.name: Second
nodes.currentDefinition: Defined by fixing the numerical value of the caesium frequency Δν_Cs, the unperturbed ground-state hyperfine transition frequency of the caesium-133 atom, to 9,192,631,770 hertz, where the hertz is s⁻¹.

nodes.etymology: From Latin 'secunda pars minuta', 'second small part' (of an hour), following 'prima pars minuta', the minute.
nodes.cursedness: Since 2019 the definition fixes the caesium frequency in hertz, 'which is equal to s⁻¹', so the second is defined through a unit built from the second. The IEC's terminology committee used the second as its main example of how the 2019 definitions read circularly: the caesium frequency is stated in a unit made of seconds, and the second is defined by that frequency. They concluded the definition is still sound, since fixing the number pins the second to the caesium atom, but that its wording can't be copied verbatim into a terminology standard (Mari et al., 2019). The rewording didn't change the size of the second; it only restated the 1967 definition as a fixed constant, like the other six base units.

nodes.name: Slug

nodes.name: Steradian

nodes.etymology: From Greek 'stereos' (solid) + 'radian'.

links.note:
The Fahrenheit scale is now defined from the Celsius scale, which is
defined from the kelvin: t/°F = 1.8 · t/°C + 32. Both are offset scales.
A degree Fahrenheit is 5/9 of a degree Celsius, and their zeros differ:
0 °F is about −17.8 °C. They cross at −40, where −40 °F = −40 °C. The
Rankine scale does for Fahrenheit what the kelvin does for Celsius: it
keeps the degree size and moves zero to absolute zero, at −459.67 °F.
links.sourceRef: NIST Handbook 44, Appendix C; BIPM SI Brochure, 9th ed. (2019), sec. 2.3.4.

links.note:
When the US adopted the international foot (0.3048 m) in 1959, it kept the
old foot of 1200/3937 m for geodetic surveying, so as not to change decades
of survey records. The two differ by 2 parts per million, about 3.2 mm in a
mile. That is invisible on a building site but adds up across a State Plane
coordinate grid, and states disagreed over which foot their grids used.
NIST, NOAA and the National Geodetic Survey deprecated the survey foot
from 1 January 2023.
links.sourceRef: Federal Register 24 FR 5348 (1959); Federal Register 85 FR 62698 (2020).

links.note:
The gray and the sievert are both one joule per kilogram, but they measure
different things. The gray is absorbed dose: the physical energy that
ionizing radiation deposits in each kilogram of matter. The sievert is dose
equivalent: that absorbed dose multiplied by dimensionless weighting
factors for how harmful the radiation type is (20 for alpha particles, 1
for gamma rays) and how sensitive the tissue is. So 1 Gy of alpha radiation
to an organ is 20 Sv of equivalent dose. Since the factors are numbers, the
units stay the same, and only the name tells you which quantity you have.
The SI Brochure insists the name always be given rather than writing J/kg.
links.sourceRef: CIPM (2002), Recommendation 2; BIPM SI Brochure, 9th ed. (2019), Table 4; ICRP Publication 103 (2007).

links.note:
The hertz and the becquerel are both the reciprocal second (s⁻¹), but the
SI never lets one stand in for the other. The hertz is for periodic
phenomena: a wave or oscillation completing one cycle per second. The
becquerel is for radioactive activity: on average one random nuclear decay
per second, with no period at all. The CGPM gave activity its own name in
1975 because writing "s⁻¹" or "Hz" for a radiation source invites mistakes
that could endanger human health. Angular velocity (rad/s) is a third
quantity with the same dimension, and the SI keeps it out of hertz too.
links.sourceRef: 15th CGPM (1975), Resolution 8; BIPM SI Brochure, 9th ed. (2019), sec. 2.3.4.

links.note:
The kelvin and the degree Celsius are the same size — a change of 1 K equals
a change of 1 °C — they only differ in where zero sits: 0 K is absolute
zero, while 0 °C is set at 273.15 K (the ice point of water). Historically,
temperature and heat were conflated for a long time, and Anders Celsius's
original 1742 proposal even ran the scale backwards from today's (0 at the
boiling point of water, 100 at freezing) before it was inverted shortly
after his death. The 2019 redefinition of the kelvin via the Boltzmann
constant left the Celsius scale's offset definition untouched, so Celsius
is now formally defined as an offset SI-derived unit built directly on the
kelvin rather than as its own independent base quantity.
links.sourceRef: BIPM SI Brochure, 9th ed. (2019), sec. 2.3.4 and Annex.

links.note:
"Pound" names both a mass (0.453 592 37 kg) and the force that mass weighs
under standard gravity (about 4.448 N), and both are routinely written
"lb". Engineering formulas then need a conversion constant, g_c =
32.174 lb·ft/(lbf·s²), to make F = ma work. Alternatives were invented to
avoid it: the slug, a mass unit that pairs with the pound-force, and the
poundal, a force unit that pairs with the pound. In 1999 NASA lost the Mars
Climate Orbiter after Lockheed Martin's ground software reported thruster
impulse in pound-force seconds and NASA's navigation software read the
numbers as newton-seconds, a factor of 4.45 off.
links.sourceRef: Mars Climate Orbiter Mishap Investigation Board, Phase I Report (NASA, 1999); NIST Handbook 44, Appendix C.

links.note:
Three masses share the name "ton": the British long ton of 2240 lb
(1016.05 kg), the metric tonne of 1000 kg, and the American short ton of
2000 lb (907.18 kg). They come from the same root, the "tun" wine cask. The
long ton and the tonne are within 1.6 % of each other, close enough to be
confused in shipping contracts. In the US, the tonne is officially the
"metric ton".
links.sourceRef: NIST Handbook 44, Appendix C; Weights and Measures Act 1985 (UK), Schedule 1.

links.note:
The US gallon (231 in³, about 3.785 L) is Queen Anne's wine gallon of
1707, which the American colonies were using when they left. In 1824
Britain replaced its wine, ale and corn gallons with one new imperial
gallon, defined as 10 pounds of water (about 4.546 L). The two have been
different ever since: an imperial gallon is about 1.2 US gallons. Every
smaller unit inherits the gap differently, because the imperial pint holds
20 fluid ounces and the US pint 16. The imperial fluid ounce is about 4 %
smaller than the US one, yet the imperial pint is about 20 % larger.
links.sourceRef: Weights and Measures Act 1824; Weights and Measures Act 1985 (UK), Schedule 1; NIST Handbook 44, Appendix C.
